Adverse effects and precautions. ENTERAL NUTRITION. Complications of enteral feeding can arise from mechanical, gastrointestinal, metabolic or other causes, such as infection or aspiration.1 The most common nutritional complication of enteral feeding is failure to meet nutritional requirements, and overzealous feeding may lead to the ‘refeeding syndrome’ manifested by glucose intolerance, fluid retention, and elec- trolyte imbalances.2 High-protein formulas with low water in- take may also cause this syndrome.1 These rapid metabolic and electrolyte changes can lead to severe or even fatal cardi- opulmonary and neurological problems.3 To avoid these problems, low levels of feeding for the first few days have been recommended; about 20 kcal/kg daily has been suggest- ed but even this may be too high, especially in patients with existing electrolyte abnormalities, and about 10 kcal/kg daily may be more suitable for high-risk patients.4 Mechanical or physical complications include displacement or clogging of the tube, or patient discomfort.1-5 Many of the problems en- countered can be avoided by using a fine bore tube, giving the feed by continuous infusion, and by careful monitoring of the patient for metabolic abnormalities.6 However, tubes become clogged more often if the calibre of the tube is small, the tube is long, placed in the stomach, the feeding continuous, or if medication is given through the tube.2,5 Inadequate flushing and protein precipitation may also occur.3 Positioning the tube in the small bowel rather than the stomach has been suggested to reduce the incidence of aspiration,2,5,7 al- though few studies have been done comparing intraduodenal and intragastric feeding in terms of clinical outcomes, and there are concerns about appropriate placement, infection, and reflux.8 A meta-analysis9 failed to find any clinical benefit of post-pyloric feeding over gastric feeding in terms of the incidence of pneumo- nia, length of stay, and mortality; the study was limited by a rel- atively small number of patients, and did not include patients considered at high risk of aspiration.
